outcome: Hales and Vajjha (arXiv, May 2024) proved Mahler's First conjecture (1947): the most unpackable centrally-symmetric convex disk in the plane must be a smoothed polygon. This narrows the class of candidate minimizers for Reinhardt's conjecture but does not identify the minimizer as specifically the smoothed octagon (Mahler's Second conjecture, equivalent to Reinhardt's conjecture), which remains open.
summary: Reinhardt's conjecture (1934) itself remains open: no source found since 26 January 2024 identifies the smoothed octagon as the packing-density minimizer among centrally-symmetric convex plane sets. What did happen in the window is a narrowing of the candidate class. A 260-page arXiv preprint/book by Thomas Hales and Koundinya Vajjha, 'Packings of Smoothed Polygons' (arXiv:2405.04331, posted 7 May 2024), proves Mahler's First conjecture (1947): that the extreme (most unpackable) centrally-symmetric convex domain must be a smoothed polygon — i.e. a polygon with corners rounded by hyperbolic arcs. This is a genuine restriction on the space of candidate minimizers for the same optimization problem that Reinhardt's conjecture concerns, so under this task's scope rule (§3.1) it counts as a case/partial result on the parent question rather than an unrelated variant: it removes territory (non-smoothed-polygon shapes) from consideration as the minimizer. It does not, however, settle which smoothed polygon (i.e., whether it is the octagon specifically) is optimal — Mahler's Second conjecture, equivalent to the Reinhardt conjecture as stated in the bullet, is untouched. Quanta Magazine (28 June 2024) and other secondary coverage (Brian Hayes' blog, Mathstodon, a 2024-11-01 Visual Insight post) confirm this reading and report informal expert engagement: Henry Cohn (Microsoft Research) and Greg Kuperberg (UC Davis) reviewed parts of the argument favorably, with Kuperberg explicitly noting the authors 'didn't really cross the finish line' toward the full Reinhardt conjecture. As of this research (September 2026), I found no evidence the 260-page proof has completed formal peer review or journal publication, nor a full third-party expert digestion working through the entire proof (only partial/informal review by named mathematicians is documented) — so I classify the underlying event as not yet fully 'resolved' by the §6.1 standard, though the informal expert engagement is substantial. Since the record concerns the parent conjecture (not Mahler's First conjecture as its own bullet), and only a sub-case/restriction was settled, 'status' is 'partial' rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed'. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the primary source, in Quanta's coverage, or in any other secondary source I found. The paper describes 'computer-assisted' proofs using a computer algebra system for verifying certain polynomial/algebraic inequalities — this is symbolic computation, not a machine-learning or AI system, so 'ai_role' is 'none' per §6.2's explicit carve-out for computer algebra and certified computation. I also searched for any later work (2025-2026) advancing toward identifying the octagon itself, or any AI-related attempt at Reinhardt's conjecture, and found none: search results consistently point back to the same May 2024 preprint as the most recent development, alongside an unrelated 2026 paper on a different 'Yau's conjecture on smooth Reinhardt domains' (a complex-analysis topic with only a name in common, not related to this packing conjecture).
competing_reading: One could argue the Hales-Vajjha result is a 'related problem' (Mahler's First conjecture) rather than a 'case' of Reinhardt's conjecture, since it is formally a distinct named conjecture with its own history (posed by Mahler in 1947, separate from Reinhardt's 1934 conjecture) and could be classified as 'open' with 'no_change_found' true, treating the Hales-Vajjha work as beside the specific question of whether the octagon is optimal. However, the two conjectures are widely treated in the literature (Wikipedia's own smoothed-octagon article, Quanta) as sequential steps toward the same optimization problem — Mahler's First and Second conjectures are the two halves of establishing that the octagon is optimal — so I favor 'partial' since the result strictly narrows the feasible set for the object Reinhardt's conjecture is about.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that among smoothed polygons specifically, the smoothed octagon (as opposed to a smoothed polygon with a different number of sides) minimizes packing density — i.e., a resolution of Mahler's Second conjecture / Reinhardt's conjecture itself. Also relevant: formal peer-review publication or a complete independent expert re-derivation of the Hales-Vajjha proof, which would move that underlying result from informally-vetted preprint status to fully digested.

events.what: Hales and Vajjha prove Mahler's First conjecture: the most unpackable centrally-symmetric convex disk is a smoothed polygon

judgement.doubts: Scope is the judgement call. The result shows the minimizer lies among smoothed polygons, but it does not show that any class of shapes has density at least that of the smoothed octagon, so no restriction of the bullet's question is settled. It reduces Reinhardt's conjecture to Mahler's Second conjecture, which is still open (Kuperberg, as quoted in the record: 'didn't really cross the finish line'). That makes it a reduction (scope none), not a case. A reader who counts narrowing the candidate class as a case would code this partial. Named informal expert reading (Cohn, Kuperberg) covered parts of the argument only.
